nodes.name: Unit fraction as one of b equal parts of a whole
nodes.statement: 1/b names the quantity formed by one part when a whole is partitioned into b equal parts.
nodes.assess: This rectangle is split into 6 equal parts and one is shaded. What fraction of the rectangle is shaded?

proposed_edges.rationale: The phrase 'b equal parts' means parts of equal area, for any whole number b, not only 2, 3 or 4.
The whole is partitioned into b equal parts, which is the equal-shares partition of a circle or rectangle.
The unit fraction 1/b generalizes the names half, third and fourth to any b, naming one equal share.
The denominator b counts all the equal parts that together make the whole, which is why one part is 1/b.

nodes.name: Non-unit fraction as a parts of size 1/b
nodes.statement: a/b names the quantity formed by a parts, each of size 1/b, of a whole partitioned into b equal parts.
nodes.assess: A bar is split into 8 equal parts and 3 are shaded. What fraction of the bar is shaded?

proposed_edges.rationale: The numerator a is the count of parts of size 1/b that are taken, found by counting them.
The statement defines a/b as a parts each of size 1/b, so the unit fraction 1/b must already be meaningful.

nodes.name: Locate a unit fraction on the number line
nodes.statement: 1/b is the point reached by partitioning the interval from 0 to 1 into b equal lengths and taking one of those lengths from 0.
nodes.assess: Place 1/4 on a number line marked only with 0 and 1.
procedure: Mark 0 and 1 on a number line.
Partition the interval from 0 to 1 into b equal lengths.
Label the endpoint of the first length from 0 as 1/b.

proposed_edges.rationale: Step 3 labels the first of b equal lengths as 1/b, carrying over the meaning of a unit fraction as one of b equal parts.
Step 1 marks 0 and 1 on a number line, so the learner must read the length from 0 to 1 as one unit.
Step 2 splits the interval from 0 to 1 into b equal lengths, the same equal-length partition of a side used there.

nodes.name: Locate a non-unit fraction on the number line
nodes.statement: a/b is the endpoint reached by marking off a lengths of size 1/b from 0 on the number line.
nodes.assess: Place 5/6 on a number line marked only with 0 and 1.
procedure: Locate 1/b on the number line.
Mark off a copies of the length 1/b, end to end, starting at 0.
Label the endpoint of the last copy as a/b.

proposed_edges.rationale: The statement reads a/b as a copies of size 1/b, the same meaning as a parts each of size 1/b.
Step 1 locates 1/b on the number line, which gives the length that is then copied a times.
Step 2 lays a copies of the length 1/b end to end from 0 with no gaps or overlaps, as in iterating a unit.

nodes.name: A fraction is a number
nodes.statement: A fraction names a single point on the number line, so it is a number of the same kind as a whole number, with a definite size and position.
nodes.assess: Is 3/4 more than 0? Less than 1? Mark where it goes between 0 and 2.

proposed_edges.rationale: The claim that a fraction names a single point rests on being able to locate a/b by marking off lengths from 0.
Calling a fraction a number of the same kind as a whole number requires whole numbers already seen as points on the line.

nodes.name: Whole numbers written as fractions
nodes.statement: Any whole number can be written as a fraction: n = n/1, and 1 = b/b for any b, because both name the same point on the number line.
nodes.assess: Write 3 as a fraction. Write 1 as a fraction with denominator 6.

proposed_edges.rationale: Saying two fractions are one number because they name the same point needs fractions understood as numbers with positions.
The reason b/b equals 1 is that marking off b lengths of 1/b from 0 lands exactly at the point 1.
Writing n as n/1 compares the fraction point with the whole-number point n reached by n unit lengths from 0.

nodes.name: Equivalent fractions as the same amount of the same whole
nodes.statement: Two fractions are equivalent when they cover the same amount of the same whole.
nodes.assess: These two equal-size bars show 1/2 and 2/4 shaded. Are the fractions equal? How do you know?

proposed_edges.rationale: Deciding that two shaded regions cover the same amount of the same whole uses direct comparison of area.
Each of the two fractions being compared is read as a parts of size 1/b of a whole.
The same amount can be cut into differently sized and shaped parts, as with 1/2 and 2/4 of equal bars.

nodes.name: Equivalent fractions as the same point on the number line
nodes.statement: Two fractions are equivalent when they name the same point on the number line.
nodes.assess: On this number line, 2/3 and 4/6 are marked. Are they equivalent? How do you know?

proposed_edges.rationale: Two fractions can name the same point only if each fraction is already understood as a point with a definite position.
The number-line model locates each fraction such as 2/3 and 4/6 by marking off lengths of its unit fraction from 0.

nodes.name: Recognize and generate simple equivalent fractions with a model
nodes.statement: Using a fraction model with denominators 2, 3, 4, 6, or 8, find a fraction that covers the same amount as a given one by splitting or joining its parts.
nodes.assess: Use a fraction strip to find a fraction equal to 2/3 with denominator 6.
procedure: Show the given fraction on a model.
Split each part into equal smaller parts, or join equal groups of parts.
Count the new number of shaded parts and total parts and write the new fraction.

proposed_edges.rationale: Step 3 counts the new number of shaded parts and of total parts in order to write the new fraction.
The new fraction is accepted because it covers the same amount of the same whole as the given one.
Step 1 shows the given fraction on a model as a shaded parts out of b equal parts, and step 3 writes the new one.
Step 2 splits each part into equal smaller parts, which is partitioning a shape into equal shares.

nodes.name: Explain why simple equivalent fractions are equal
nodes.statement: For a specific pair such as 1/2 and 2/4, a model shows the two fractions cover the same amount of the same whole, so they are equal.
nodes.assess: Explain, with a drawing, why 1/2 = 2/4.

proposed_edges.rationale: The explanation concludes that 1/2 and 2/4 are equal because the model shows the same amount of the same whole.
The explanation accounts for what splitting each part in the model produces, the step of generating an equivalent fraction.
The drawing has to show 2/4 as two shaded parts out of four equal parts of the whole.

nodes.name: Compare fractions with the same denominator
nodes.statement: When two fractions have the same denominator, the parts are the same size, so the fraction with more parts is greater.
nodes.assess: Which is greater, 3/8 or 5/8? Explain.

proposed_edges.rationale: With equal part sizes the decision reduces to comparing the two numerators as whole numbers, such as 3 and 5.
Saying one fraction is greater requires that fractions have definite sizes that can be ordered like whole numbers.
Each fraction a/b is a lengths of size 1/b from 0, so the one with more lengths lies farther along the line.
Each fraction is a parts of one common size 1/b, so equal denominators leave only the number of parts to compare.

nodes.name: Compare fractions with the same numerator
nodes.statement: When two fractions have the same numerator, there are the same number of parts, so the fraction whose parts are larger (smaller denominator) is greater.
nodes.assess: Which is greater, 2/3 or 2/5? Explain.

proposed_edges.rationale: Finding which denominator is smaller, such as 3 versus 5, compares two whole numbers.
The statement reads each fraction as the same number of parts of size 1/b, so the part size is all that differs.
A larger denominator means more equal shares of the whole, so each part is smaller, which decides the comparison.

nodes.name: Compare fractions by reasoning about their size
nodes.statement: Decide which of two fractions is greater by reasoning about the size of the parts and how many there are.
nodes.assess: Which is greater, 3/4 or 3/6? Which is greater, 2/6 or 5/6?

proposed_edges.rationale: The test pairs such as 2/6 and 5/6 are decided by counting how many parts of equal size each fraction has.
The test pairs such as 3/4 and 3/6 are decided by comparing the size of the parts when the part counts match.

nodes.name: Fraction comparisons need the same whole
nodes.statement: Comparing two fractions by size is only valid when both refer to the same whole; 1/2 of a small pizza can be less than 1/3 of a large one.
nodes.assess: Sam says 1/2 is always bigger than 1/3. When could 1/3 of something be bigger than 1/2 of something?

proposed_edges.rationale: The small pizza versus large pizza example is settled by directly comparing the two actual amounts of pizza.
The caveat qualifies the rule that 1/2 is greater than 1/3, which is reasoning about part size and number of parts.
A fraction such as 1/2 names one part of some particular whole, so its actual amount depends on which whole is meant.

nodes.name: Record fraction comparisons with >, =, <
nodes.statement: The result of comparing two fractions is written with the symbols >, =, or <.
nodes.assess: Write >, =, or < between 4/6 and 2/6.

proposed_edges.rationale: The symbols >, = and < are the same ones already used to record comparisons of whole numbers.
The symbol written records the outcome of a comparison, which must first be decided by reasoning about the two fractions.

nodes.name: Justify a fraction comparison
nodes.statement: A comparison of fractions with the same numerator or the same denominator is justified by a model or an argument about part size and number of parts.
nodes.assess: Use a drawing to show why 2/3 > 2/5.

proposed_edges.rationale: The argument about number of equal-size parts is the justification of the same-denominator comparison.
The argument about part size when the part counts match is the justification of the same-numerator comparison.
A drawing comparing two fractions is valid only if both models use wholes of the same size, as in the 2/3 versus 2/5 drawing.
The drawing shows each fraction as a number of shaded equal parts out of the total number of parts.

nodes.name: Compare fractions in a story about shares
nodes.statement: A story problem gives two fractional shares of same-size wholes; the learner decides which share is larger and explains why.
nodes.assess: Ana ate 2/6 of a pizza and Ben ate 2/8 of a pizza the same size. Who ate more? Explain.

proposed_edges.rationale: The learner must also explain why one share is larger, using a model or an argument about part size.
The learner decides which of two shares such as 2/6 and 2/8 is larger by reasoning about part size and count.
The story states that the pizzas are the same size, which is the condition that makes the comparison valid.

nodes.name: The multiplication principle for equivalent fractions
nodes.statement: For any fraction a/b and any whole number n greater than 0, a/b = (n x a)/(n x b).
nodes.assess: True or false: 3/5 = 12/20. True or false: 3/5 = 5/7. Say which rule decides it.

proposed_edges.rationale: The rule asserts that a/b and (n x a)/(n x b) name the same point, which is what equivalence means on the line.
The rule is the general symbolic form of the pattern seen when splitting every part in a model into equal smaller parts.
The products n x a and n x b are totals of n equal groups of a parts and of b parts.
Checking that 12/20 equals 3/5 requires multiplying 3 and 5 by 4 using single-digit facts.

nodes.name: Generate equivalent fractions with a/b = (n x a)/(n x b)
nodes.statement: Produce a fraction equivalent to a/b by multiplying its numerator and denominator by the same whole number n greater than 0.
nodes.assess: Write two fractions equivalent to 3/5.
procedure: Choose a whole number n greater than 0.
Multiply the numerator by n and the denominator by n.
Write the result as the equivalent fraction.

proposed_edges.rationale: The result is accepted as equivalent to a/b because of the rule a/b = (n x a)/(n x b).
Step 2 multiplies the numerator and the denominator by n, for example 3 x 2 and 5 x 2 for 3/5.

nodes.name: Recognize equivalent fractions with a/b = (n x a)/(n x b)
nodes.statement: Decide whether two fractions are equivalent by rewriting both over a common denominator with the multiplication principle and comparing numerators.
nodes.assess: Is 4/6 equivalent to 6/9? Is 6/8 equivalent to 3/5?
procedure: Find a common multiple of the two denominators.
Rewrite each fraction over that denominator by multiplying its numerator and denominator by the same whole number.
The fractions are equivalent exactly when the rewritten numerators are equal.

proposed_edges.rationale: Step 1 finds a common multiple of the two denominators, such as 18 for 6 and 9.
Step 3 says fractions over one denominator are equal exactly when numerators are equal, since more parts means a greater fraction.
The statement uses the multiplication principle to justify that each rewritten fraction equals the original.
Step 2 rewrites each fraction over the common denominator by multiplying its numerator and denominator by one whole number.

nodes.name: Explain why a/b = (n x a)/(n x b)
nodes.statement: Splitting each of the b parts into n equal parts multiplies the number of parts by n and the number of chosen parts by n, while the amount covered does not change; so (n x a)/(n x b) is the same amount as a/b, for every n.
nodes.assess: Use a visual fraction model to explain why 2/3 = (4 x 2)/(4 x 3), and say why the same argument works for any n.

proposed_edges.rationale: The explanation is for the specific equation a/b = (n x a)/(n x b), which it must state and apply for every n.
The key claim that the amount covered does not change is the meaning of two fractions covering the same whole amount.
The general argument extends the model-based explanation of why one simple pair such as 1/2 and 2/4 is equal.
Splitting each of a chosen parts into n pieces gives a groups of n, which is n x a pieces in total.
Counting b parts each split into n parts gives b x n, which equals n x b by the commutative property.

nodes.name: Partition a circle or rectangle into equal shares
nodes.statement: Divide a circle or rectangle into n shares of the same size that together make up the whole with nothing left over (in grades 1-2, n is 2, 3, or 4).
nodes.assess: Draw lines to split this rectangle into 3 equal shares.
procedure: Decide how many shares, n, are needed.
For a rectangle, draw n - 1 straight lines across it, spaced so every strip has the same width.
For a circle, draw n straight cuts from the center to the edge, spaced evenly around the center.
Check that the shares are the same size and that together they make the whole.

proposed_edges.rationale: Step 4 checks that the shares are the same size by directly comparing them.
Step 2 draws n - 1 lines and gets n strips, which requires counting lines and strips.
The statement concerns dividing a circle or a rectangle, so the learner must recognize each shape.

nodes.name: Name equal shares as halves, thirds, and fourths
nodes.statement: One of 2 equal shares of a whole is called a half of it, one of 3 equal shares a third of it, and one of 4 equal shares a fourth (or quarter) of it; the names apply only when the shares are equal.
nodes.assess: This circle is cut into 4 equal shares and one share is shaded. What word names the shaded share?

proposed_edges.rationale: Choosing the name depends on counting the equal shares, 2, 3 or 4, that the whole has been cut into.
The names half, third and fourth refer to one share of a whole divided into 2, 3 or 4 equal shares.

nodes.name: The whole as all of its equal shares
nodes.statement: A whole partitioned into n equal shares is made of exactly n of those shares: two halves, three thirds, or four fourths make one whole.
nodes.assess: A sandwich is cut into fourths. How many fourths make the whole sandwich?

proposed_edges.rationale: Finding that a sandwich cut in fourths has four fourths requires counting the shares.
The claim that n shares make up the whole with nothing left over is the property of an equal partition.
The statement is phrased with the names halves, thirds and fourths, as in two halves make one whole.

nodes.name: More equal shares of the same whole are smaller
nodes.statement: For the same whole, partitioning into more equal shares makes each share smaller; a fourth of a shape is smaller than a half of the same shape.
nodes.assess: Two crackers are the same size. One is cut into halves and the other into fourths. Which is bigger, a half or a fourth?

proposed_edges.rationale: Deciding that one share is smaller than another share of the same whole uses direct comparison of size.
The statement compares the shares from partitioning the same whole into different numbers of equal shares.
The test compares a half with a fourth, so the learner must know those share names.
The shares always together make the same whole, so more shares means each takes a smaller part.

nodes.name: Equal shares need not have the same shape
nodes.statement: Shares of identical wholes are equal when they cover the same amount, even if they have different shapes.
nodes.assess: Two identical squares are each cut in half, one along a diagonal into triangles and one straight down the middle into rectangles. Is a triangle half the same amount as a rectangle half?

proposed_edges.rationale: Judging that shares cover the same amount even though their shapes differ uses direct comparison of amount of area.
The statement concerns shares produced by different ways of partitioning identical wholes into equal shares.
The test asks whether a triangle half equals a rectangle half, so the learner must know what a half is.
The statement contrasts shares of different shapes, such as triangles and rectangles cut from identical squares.

nodes.name: Partition a shape into parts with equal area
nodes.statement: Partition a shape into n parts that have the same area, checking equality by area (for example by counting unit squares) rather than by shape. The steps below work for any rectangle and any n; other shapes are split into pieces whose areas are then checked to be equal.
nodes.assess: This 6-by-2 rectangle is drawn on a grid. Partition it into 6 parts with equal area and show how you know the areas are equal.
procedure: For a rectangle, partition one side into n equal lengths.
Through each mark, draw a line parallel to the adjacent side, making n strips.
Confirm the strips have equal area (same length and width, or the same number of unit squares).

proposed_edges.rationale: Equality of the parts is checked by area, counting unit squares or using length times width of each strip.
Step 1 partitions one side into n equal lengths by laying equal unit lengths along it.
Step 1 divides one side of a rectangle into n equal lengths, extending to any n the equal strips drawn there.
The statement says equality is checked by area rather than by shape, since equal parts may have different shapes.

nodes.name: Length as the number of units that span an object
nodes.statement: The length of an object in a given unit is the number of same-size copies of that unit that span it end to end with no gaps and no overlaps.
nodes.assess: Mia laid paper clips along a pencil with spaces between them and counted 5. Is the pencil 5 paper clips long? Why or why not?

proposed_edges.rationale: Spanning the object end to end with same-size copies uses direct comparison of lengths to match endpoints and unit sizes.
The length is the number of unit copies, which is found by counting them.

nodes.name: Measure length by laying units end to end
nodes.statement: Measure an object's length by laying same-size copies of a shorter unit end to end along it and counting them. At this level objects are chosen to be a whole number of units long; if the last copy overhangs the end, the length lies between two whole numbers of units.
nodes.assess: Use copies of this paper clip to find how long the marker is, in paper clips.
procedure: Line up one end of the first copy of the unit with one end of the object.
Place each next copy so it starts exactly where the previous one ends, in a straight line along the object, with no gap and no overlap.
Stop when a copy reaches the other end of the object.
Count the copies; that whole number is the length in that unit.

proposed_edges.rationale: The unit is shorter than the object and the last copy reaches or overhangs the end, which is judged by direct comparison.
Step 4 counts the copies to get the whole-number length.
Step 2 places each copy exactly where the previous one ends, with no gap and no overlap, which is the meaning of length.

nodes.name: Whole numbers as lengths from 0 on a number line
nodes.statement: On a number line diagram with equally spaced points labeled 0, 1, 2, ..., the whole number n is represented by the length from 0 to the point labeled n, which is n unit lengths.
nodes.assess: On this number line, draw the length that shows 7.

proposed_edges.rationale: The labels 0, 1, 2, ... are the counting numbers assigned to equally spaced points on the line.
Drawing the length for 7 means laying seven unit lengths end to end starting at 0.
The length from 0 to n is read as n same-size unit lengths spanning with no gaps or overlaps.

nodes.name: Represent a whole-number sum on a number line
nodes.statement: The sum a + b is shown on a number line by placing a length of b units end to end after the length from 0 to a; the endpoint is a + b.
nodes.assess: Show 38 + 25 on a number line and find the sum.
procedure: Mark the length from 0 to a.
From a, mark a further length of b units to the right, in one jump or in smaller jumps that total b.
Read the label at the endpoint; it is a + b.

proposed_edges.rationale: The model must represent the meaning of a + b as the total from joining a and b, and the endpoint is read as the sum.
Placing the length b end to end after the length a relies on lengths joining with no gaps and no overlaps.
Step 1 marks the length from 0 to a, which is the whole number a shown as a length on the line.
Step 2 splits b into smaller jumps that total b, such as 20 and 5 for 25, using tens and ones.

nodes.name: Represent a whole-number difference by jumping back on a number line
nodes.statement: For whole numbers with b no greater than a, the difference a - b is shown by starting at a and moving b units to the left; the point reached is a - b.
nodes.assess: Show 62 - 17 on a number line by jumping back from 62, and find the difference.
procedure: Locate a on the number line.
From a, mark a length of b units to the left, in one jump or in smaller jumps that total b.
Read the label at the endpoint; it is a - b.

proposed_edges.rationale: Step 1 locates a on the number line, the point reached by a unit lengths from 0.
Step 2 splits the jump of b units into smaller jumps, such as 10 and 7 for 17, using tens and ones.
The model represents a - b as what remains when b is taken away from a, so that meaning of subtraction is used.

nodes.name: Represent a whole-number difference as a distance on a number line
nodes.statement: For whole numbers with b no greater than a, the difference a - b is the length of the segment from b to a on the number line.
nodes.assess: Use a number line to find how far it is from 48 to 73, and write the subtraction it shows.
procedure: Locate b and a on the number line.
Measure the length from b up to a, in one jump or in smaller jumps (for example to the next ten, then by tens).
The total length of the jumps is a - b.

proposed_edges.rationale: Step 3 adds the lengths of the jumps to get the total distance.
The difference is read as how much longer one quantity is than the other, a direct comparison of two lengths.
Step 2 measures the length of the segment from b to a as a count of unit lengths spanning it.
Step 1 locates both b and a as points on the number line, each marked by its length from 0.
Step 2 jumps from b to the next ten and then by tens, which uses the tens and ones structure of the numbers.
The statement says the length of the segment is a - b, so the meaning of subtraction is needed to name that length.

nodes.name: A product as a number of equal groups
nodes.statement: For whole numbers a and b, a x b is the total number of objects in a groups with b objects in each group.
nodes.assess: In 5 x 7 = 35, counting objects in groups, what does the 5 stand for, what does the 7 stand for, and what does the 35 stand for?

proposed_edges.rationale: The total of a groups with b objects each is found by joining the groups, which is a sum of a equal addends.
The product is a total number of objects, and a and b are counts of groups and of objects in each group.

nodes.name: Match a multiplication expression to an equal-groups situation
nodes.statement: Given a x b, identify or describe a situation with a groups of b objects each whose total the expression gives.
nodes.assess: Which story is about 4 x 6? (A) 4 bags with 6 apples in each bag. (B) 4 apples and 6 more apples. (C) 6 apples shared among 4 bags.

proposed_edges.rationale: The learner must read a x b as a groups of b objects each in order to pick or invent the matching situation.

nodes.name: Model an equal-groups situation and write a multiplication expression
nodes.statement: Represent an equal-groups situation with objects or a drawing and write it as a x b, where a is the number of groups and b is the number in each group.
nodes.assess: There are 7 boxes with 3 crayons in each box. Draw a picture and write a multiplication expression for the total number of crayons.

proposed_edges.rationale: Writing a x b for 7 boxes of 3 crayons requires knowing a is the number of groups and b the number in each group.

nodes.name: A quotient as the size of each equal share
nodes.statement: When a objects are partitioned equally into b groups, the quotient a divided by b is the number of objects in each group.
nodes.assess: 24 stickers are shared equally among 6 children, and 24 divided by 6 is 4. What does the 4 tell you?

proposed_edges.rationale: The quotient is a count of the objects in each group, found by counting the objects shared out.
The b groups made by sharing are equal groups, so the quotient is the group size that makes b equal groups total a.

nodes.name: A quotient as the number of equal groups
nodes.statement: When a objects are put into equal groups of b objects each, the quotient a divided by b is the number of groups.
nodes.assess: 24 stickers are put into packs of 6, and 24 divided by 6 is 4. What does the 4 tell you?

proposed_edges.rationale: The quotient is a count of the groups formed, such as the 4 packs of 6 stickers.
The groups of b objects are equal groups, so the quotient is the number of such equal groups that total a.

nodes.name: Model a sharing situation and write a division expression
nodes.statement: Represent a situation in which a objects are shared equally among b groups, with the size of each group unknown, using objects or a drawing, and write it as a divided by b.
nodes.assess: 18 apples are shared equally among 3 baskets. Draw a picture and write a division expression for the number of apples in each basket.

proposed_edges.rationale: Writing a divided by b for a sharing situation requires knowing the quotient is the number in each group.

nodes.name: Model a grouping situation and write a division expression
nodes.statement: Represent a situation in which a objects are put into groups of b, with the number of groups unknown, using objects or a drawing, and write it as a divided by b.
nodes.assess: 18 apples are packed 3 to a bag. Draw a picture and write a division expression for the number of bags.

proposed_edges.rationale: Writing a divided by b for a grouping situation requires knowing the quotient is the number of groups.

nodes.name: Match a division expression to a sharing situation
nodes.statement: Given a divided by b, identify or describe a situation in which a objects are shared equally among b groups and the quotient is the number in each group.
nodes.assess: Write a story in which 20 divided by 4 tells how many are in each group.

proposed_edges.rationale: Inventing a story where 20 divided by 4 gives the number in each group uses the sharing meaning of the quotient.

nodes.name: Match a division expression to a grouping situation
nodes.statement: Given a divided by b, identify or describe a situation in which a objects are put into groups of b and the quotient is the number of groups.
nodes.assess: Write a story in which 20 divided by 4 tells how many groups there are.

proposed_edges.rationale: Inventing a story where 20 divided by 4 gives the number of groups uses the grouping meaning of the quotient.

nodes.name: A quotient as an unknown factor
nodes.statement: For whole numbers a and b, with b not 0 and a a multiple of b, a divided by b is the whole number c for which b x c = a.
nodes.assess: Which multiplication fact shows that 42 divided by 7 is 6?

proposed_edges.rationale: Forming c groups of b from a gives c x b = a, so the number of groups c satisfies the multiplication equation.
Sharing a among b groups with c in each means b groups of c make a, so the quotient c satisfies b x c = a.
The equation b x c = a is read as b groups of c objects with a total of a objects.
Turning c groups of b into the equation b x c = a uses the commutative property of multiplication.

nodes.name: Rewrite a division problem as a multiplication with an unknown factor
nodes.statement: The division problem a divided by b = ? is rewritten as the multiplication problem b x ? = a, with the same unknown.
nodes.assess: Write 32 divided by 8 = ? as a multiplication problem with an unknown factor.

proposed_edges.rationale: Rewriting a divided by b = ? as b x ? = a applies the meaning of the quotient as the unknown factor.

nodes.name: Find a quotient by finding an unknown factor
nodes.statement: Find a divided by b by finding the unknown factor in b x ? = a. This gives a whole-number quotient only when b is not 0 and a is a multiple of b; otherwise skip-counting by b passes a without landing on it.
nodes.assess: Find 56 divided by 8 by thinking of a multiplication fact. Write the fact you used.
procedure: Rewrite a divided by b = ? as b x ? = a.
Find the whole number that makes b x ? = a true, by recalling a multiplication fact or by skip-counting by b from 0 until reaching a and counting the skips.
That number is the quotient.

proposed_edges.rationale: Naming the unknown factor as the quotient, and knowing when a whole-number quotient exists, uses the unknown-factor meaning.
Step 1 rewrites a divided by b = ? as b x ? = a before any search for the number.
Step 2 finds the number that makes b x ? = a true by recalling a single-digit multiplication fact or skip-counting by b.
